'''Classical Erotology: Corpus Catalogue, Rights Status, and Bridge Map'''

'''Status: PRIVATE / NOT PUBLISHED.''' Nothing in this file is live. No wiki article, nav
entry, category or sitemap was created or touched by the work that produced it. It is a
planning document in `.local/` for a surface that does not yet exist.

'''Date:''' 2026-10-27
'''Scope of this document:''' bibliography, history of the book, rights clearance, and the
map from this corpus to the existing Library shelves. It is a catalogue of ''texts''. It
contains no erotic or explicit content, describes no acts, and reproduces no passages
beyond bibliographic identification.

---

== Why this is the right foundation ==

The operator's framing is correct and worth stating as the governing editorial principle,
because it is also the ''legal'' and ''tonal'' principle:

# '''The classical erotological literature is scholarly, not pornographic.''' It is
   didactic, taxonomic and frequently medical. Vatsyayana writes in ''sutra'' form; the
   Arabic tradition writes in the register of the ''adab'' and the medical compendium; the
   Chinese material sits inside a dietetic-and-longevity literature. Treating it as
   bibliography is not a dodge — it is what the material actually is.
# '''Most of the underlying texts are ancient and unencumbered.''' The risk is not in the
   texts. It is in the '''translations''', and that is the entire point of Part 1's rights
   column.
# '''It connects outward.''' Roughly a third of this corpus by volume is '''formulary
   material''' — unguents, perfumes, oils, medicated foods. That is the seam with the
   Library's existing oils, preparation and chemistry shelves, mapped in Part 2.

== The rule that governs the whole catalogue ==

'''An ancient text being out of copyright does not make a modern translation of it free.'''
A translation is an original literary work in its own right and carries its own term. The
tests used throughout this document:

* '''United States:''' anything '''published before 1930''' is in the public domain
  (as of 2026 — the window advances one year each 1 January). Works published
  '''1930–1963''' entered the public domain unless the copyright was '''renewed'''; this must
  be checked case by case, and where it has not been checked this document says so.
  Works published 1964–1977 with notice: 95 years from publication. Works from 1978
  onward: life of the author + 70 years.
* '''United Kingdom / EU:''' '''life of the translator + 70 years''', regardless of
  publication date. This frequently differs from the US answer, and for the Victorian
  translators — Burton died 1890, Arbuthnot 1901, Smithers 1907 — everything clears in
  both jurisdictions.
* '''Scans and transcriptions:''' in the US, a '''faithful reproduction of a public-domain
  work generates no new copyright''' (''Bridgeman v. Corel''). A scan of an 1883 book on
  Internet Archive is therefore free in the US even where the hosting site asserts terms.
  The UK position on "sweat of the brow" in scans has historically been less settled, and
  some European institutions still assert rights over digitisations.
* '''Editorial apparatus is separate.''' A modern introduction, notes, index or critical
  edition of a public-domain translation is itself in copyright. The 1883 text is free;
  the 2003 scholar's footnotes on it are not.

Where this document could not settle a rights question, it says '''UNSETTLED''' rather than
assuming the answer is "free."

'''PART 1 — THE CORPUS, WITH RIGHTS STATUS'''

== 1.1 Sanskrit — the ''kāmaśāstra'' tradition ==

Three systemic cautions apply to this whole shelf before any individual entry:

# '''Internet Archive uploader licence tags are unreliable.''' Alex Comfort's 1964 Allen &
   Unwin ''Koka Shastra'' is tagged '''CC0 1.0''' on IA and is plainly still in copyright.
   Several 1950s–70s Indian editions carry uploader-applied CC0 with nothing behind it.
   '''Use the underlying publication date as the rights test, never the IA licence field.'''
# '''GRETIL is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0''' — the '''non-commercial clause bites''' if the host is
   commercial. GRETIL also carries a standing "will be removed pending any credible
   copyright claim" disclaimer, and at least one of its files (''Smaradīpikā'') is keyed to a
   1967 edition still in copyright.
# '''URAA restoration is the dominant rule for Indian imprints.''' A 1931–1977 Indian
   publication still protected in India on 1 Jan 1996 had its US copyright '''restored''' —
   so US renewal records are usually moot and the answer is usually "in copyright."

=== The Kama Sutra of Vātsyāyana (''Kāmasūtra'') ===

'''The text.''' Sūtra genre, prose with ''anuṣṭubh'' verse, '''seven ''adhikaraṇas'' in 36
chapters'''. Attributed to '''Vātsyāyana Mallanāga'''; nothing biographical about him is
secure. '''The date is unsettled''' — proposals run from 400 BCE to 300 CE; Keay says 2nd c.
CE; Doniger argues the second half of the '''3rd c. CE''', on the grounds that the text names
the Ābhīras and Āndhras and does not know the Guptas. The ''terminus ante quem'' is firm:
it is cited in Varāhamihira's ''Bṛhatsaṃhitā'', so it is pre-5th century.

'''The Jayamaṅgalā commentary of Yaśodhara.''' 11th–13th c., usually narrowed to the
'''11th–12th'''; the outer bound comes from a manuscript colophon naming the library of the
Chaulukya king Vīsaladeva of Gujarat (r. 1244–62). The author is '''Yaśodhara Indrapāda''';
nothing else is known of him. ⚠️ '''Disambiguation warning: at least four unrelated works
are also called ''Jayamaṅgalā''''' — commentaries on the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the Bhaṭṭikāvya, the
Arthaśāstra and Kāmandaka's Nītisāra. They will contaminate any title search.

==== The 1883 Burton/Arbuthnot translation — the authorship question, settled ====

'''Burton did not translate the Kama Sutra.''' The translation was made by '''Bhagvanlal
Indraji''' (1839 – 16 March 1888) with his student '''Shivaram Parashuram Bhide''', under
'''F. F. Arbuthnot's''' direction. '''Burton edited and revised.'''

Indraji was not an assistant — he was a serious scholar: Royal Asiatic Society Bombay, a
pioneer of Aśokan studies, and the first Indian to hold an honorary doctorate from a
foreign university (Leiden, 1884).

The evidence:
* '''Doniger''' holds it should properly be called "the Indrajit–Bhide–Arbuthnot–Burton
  translation," and that Burton's real contribution was '''the nerve to publish'''.
* '''Burton himself''' called it "Arbuthnot's Vatsyayana."
* '''Thomas Wright (1906):''' "the precise share that Burton had in them will never be
  known."
* '''The 1883 book's own introduction names no European translator.''' It records that the
  pandits obtained a defective Bombay manuscript, wrote to libraries at '''Benares,
  Calcutta and Jeypoor''', compared four copies, corrected Parts I–V against the
  '''Jayamaṅgalā''', and that the English was made from that revised copy. This can be read
  directly at <https://gutenberg.org/files/27827/27827-h/27827-h.htm>.
* In 1885 '''Arbuthnot claimed the translating was done entirely by Indian pandits''' —
  Doniger calls this a half-truth he likely knew to be false.

'''The "Kama Shastra Society of London and Benares" was a fictitious imprint, not an
organisation.''' Burton's own words: Arbuthnot "founded a society consisting of himself and
myself." Wright adds a third nominal member, '''Lord Houghton'''. Its purpose was to place
the book in '''private circulation among "members" and subscribers''' as a device around the
'''Obscene Publications Act 1857''', which made the sale of obscene matter a statutory
offence with seizure and destruction on a magistrate's information — and which, after the
1868 ''Hicklin'' test ("tendency to deprave and corrupt"), let any single passage condemn a
whole book. The imprints used — "Cosmopoli," "Benares," "London" — are all false.

'''The 1883 first edition.''' Seven parts in one volume, 8vo, title in red and black.
Imprint: *"Cosmopoli: MDCCCLXXXIII: for the Kama Shastra Society of London and Benares,
and for private circulation only."* Parts carry "Printed for the Hindoo Kama Shastra
Society"; Part I impressed "London," the rest "Benares"; two printers were used.
'''Total issue: 250 copies''' (Christie's, citing Penzer p. 163; Penzer 1923 independently
gives "The total issue was 250"). Penzer notes the parts edition "was soon exhausted, and
is now practically unobtainable."

'''First legal open publication: 1962.''' Doniger states flatly that it was '''not legally
published in England or the United States until 1962'''. The supporting imprints are
'''E. P. Dutton, New York, 1962''' and '''George Allen & Unwin, London, 1963''' (the UK trade
edition associated with W. G. Archer). ⚠️ '''The 1962/1963 US–UK split is not reconciled in
any source read; Doniger says 1962 for both.''' The enabling context: the 1857 Act was
repealed for England and Wales by the '''Obscene Publications Act 1959''', and the US
obscenity bar fell after ''Roth'' (1957) and the Grove Press cases. Between 1883 and 1962 it
was "one of the most pirated books in the English language."

'''Rights: the 1883 translation is PD worldwide.''' Published 1883; Burton d. 1890,
Arbuthnot d. 1901, Indraji d. 1888.

'''Where the 1883 text lives:'''
* '''Project Gutenberg #27827''' — <https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/27827> — credits all
  three (Bhide, Burton, Indrajit). PG states "Public domain in the USA." Full text at the
  URL above.
* '''Internet Archive `kamasutraofvatsy00vatsuoft`''' — University of Toronto / Robarts
  scan, 236 images, in the "bannedbooks" collection. No rights field; underlying text PD.
* '''English Wikisource''' — <https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Kama_Sutra_(Burton)> —
  transcribed from the above; marked '''PD worldwide''', page wrapper CC BY-SA 4.0. ⚠️ The
  source file is flagged as needing repair and '''pp. 161–163 are missing'''.
* '''Internet Archive `kamasutra_of_vatsyayama-1925`''' — IA licence '''Public Domain Mark
  1.0'''. Title page read directly: "Benares—New York… Printed for the Society of the
  Friends of India… 1883-1925… For Private Circulation Only." '''This is a pirate reprint
  of Burton, not a separate translation.'''
* '''sacred-texts.com''' — <https://sacred-texts.com/sex/kama/index.htm>. ⚠️ Site 403s
  automated fetches; URL located, page not read.
* '''Sanskrit (mūla):''' <https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/कामसूत्रम्> — complete, seven
  adhikaraṇas, '''CC BY-SA 4.0'''. Mūla only, no commentary.
* '''Sanskrit with the full Jayamaṅgalā, 1929''' —
  <https://archive.org/details/kamasutra-with-jayamangala-damodara-sastri-1929-chaukhamba>
  — Benares, Chaukhamba, 1929, OCR'd. '''PD in US.''' The best open full-text Sanskrit
  witness for the commentary.
* '''Sanskrit ''editio princeps'':''' Durgāprasāda Dvivedī, Nirṇayasāgara Press, Bombay,
  '''1891''' — the text Schmidt worked from. PD.

==== ★ The single most valuable item in this catalogue: Richard Schmidt's German ====

'''Richard Schmidt (1866–1939), *Das Kāmasūtram des Vātsyāyana… nebst dem vollständigen
Kommentare (Jayamaṅgalā) des Yaśodhara*.''' 1st ed. '''Leipzig: Wilhelm Friedrich, 1897''';
then Berlin: Hermann Barsdorf for the 3rd (1907), 5th rev. (1915), 6th (1920) and 7th
(1922); an unchanged reprint of the 5th by Decker, 1957.

'''Why it matters: it is a complete translation of both the Kāmasūtra and the full
Jayamaṅgalā — the only complete Western-language Jayamaṅgalā in existence — and it is
public domain everywhere.''' PD in the US (every edition through 1930; even on the URAA
path the 1922 expired 31 Dec 2017), and PD in Germany/EU/UK since 1 Jan 2010.

'''⚠️ And it carries the Latin veil.''' Schmidt rendered the most explicit passages into
'''Latin prose rather than German''', unannounced in his prefaces — the same convention
documented for the Bohn Martial and the early Loebs (§1.4). The evidence is twofold:
OCR of the 1915 edition shows running Latin sentence grammar (ablative absolutes,
"si autem…", "per eosdem autem…") with marker counts of ''coitus'' 152, ''atque'' 59,
''quae'' 55, ''autem'' 46; and the K10plus MARC record for the 1920 sixth edition codes
field '''041 = "ger lat"'''. Anyone using Schmidt as a free Jayamaṅgalā source needs to know
that a fraction of it is in Latin.

* Free scan: <https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.134716> (1915 5th ed.; DLI
  metadata `dc.rights: Out_of_copyright`; ⚠️ the language field is wrongly set to "eng").
  Duplicate: `in.ernet.dli.2015.142229`.
* Index of all Schmidt scans:
  <https://onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu/webbin/who/Schmidt%2c%20Richard%2c%201866%2d1939>

=== Ananga Ranga of Kalyāṇamalla ===

'''The text.''' ''Anaṅgaraṅga'' ("Stage of the Bodiless One"), also ''Kamaledhiplava''.
'''15th–16th c.''' Author '''Kalyāṇamalla''', writing for '''Lād Khān''', son of Ahmed Khān Lodī
of the Delhi Lodī line (1451–1526). (The variant "Ladakhana" is not supported.)

'''The 1873 suppressed printing — settled, from Penzer's 1923 bibliography read directly.'''
* The 1873 title page read: '''''Kama-Shastra, or The Hindoo Art of Love (Ars Amoris
  Indica). Translated from the Sanskrit, and Annotated by A. F. F. and B. F. R.''''' —
  Burton's and Arbuthnot's initials, deliberately garbled.
* '''Only four or six copies were printed.'''
* '''Why it stopped:''' Penzer quotes Burton's own ''Index Librorum Prohibitorum'' — the
  printer "became alarmed at the nature of the book, and refused to print off the
  edition." '''Penzer does not say copies were destroyed.'''
* The rough proofs surfaced at auction in '''March 1902''', selling for '''£3'''.
* Source, PD and full text: <https://archive.org/details/32882019070484-anannotatedbibl>
  — N. M. Penzer, ''An Annotated Bibliography of Sir Richard Francis Burton'' (1923), Kama
  Shastra Society section, pp. ~162–173.

'''The 1885 edition.''' Reissued under the new title, imprint *"Cosmopoli: MDCCCLXXXV: for
the Kama Shastra Society of London and Benares, and for private circulation only."* The
first 1885 printing sold out and two further reprints followed. '''No print-run figure is
recorded for 1885''' — the only run Penzer states is the 1873 four-or-six. Separately:
'''Isabel Burton burned the manuscript of the translation and notes after Burton's death in
1890.''' Of seven erotic works the Society planned, '''only two appeared''' — the *Kama
Sutra* and the ''Ananga Ranga''.

'''Rights: PD worldwide.'''

'''Where it lives:'''
* ★ '''Internet Archive `0327725.nlm.nih.gov`''' —
  <https://archive.org/details/0327725.nlm.nih.gov> — '''the 1885 first edition itself''',
  publisher field verbatim "Cosmopoli [England?]: For the Kama Shastra Society of London
  and Benares, and for private circulation only," xvi+144 pp, US National Library of
  Medicine / Open Knowledge Commons, digitised 2017. '''Full text, PDF and EPUB all
  available. Best source.'''
* '''English Wikisource index''' — <https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Index:Ananga-Ranga.djvu>
  — the 1885 Cosmopoli scan. ⚠️ '''Not proofread, not transcluded — no readable mainspace
  text yet.''' (A worthwhile contribution target.)
* '''sacred-texts.com''' — <https://sacred-texts.com/sex/ar/index.htm>. ⚠️ 403s to automated
  fetch; URL located, page not read.
* '''Sanskrit:''' `in.ernet.dli.2015.369655` (Lahore, 1927). ⚠️ DLI `dc.rights` reads
  '''"IN_COPYRIGHT"''' on this item — probably over-cautious for a 1927 imprint, but flagged
  as the record states it. '''Not on GRETIL; not on sa.wikisource.'''
* ⚠️ `dli.venugopal.724` is catalogued '''1880''', which is almost certainly a DLI metadata
  error — no 1880 edition is known. Unverified.

=== Ratirahasya / Koka Shastra of Kokkoka ===

'''The text.''' ''Ratirahasya'' ("Secret of Love"), popularly the ''Koka Śāstra'' after its
author. 15 chapters. ⚠️ '''Date unsettled''' — Internet Archive cataloguing says 8th c.,
Wikipedia's kāmaśāstra survey says 11th–12th (and 13th elsewhere in the same article).

'''The translation.''' '''Alex Comfort''' (translation and introduction), preface by '''W. G.
Archer''' — *The Koka Shastra, Being the Ratirahasya of Kokkoka, and Other Medieval Indian
Writings on Love*, '''London: George Allen & Unwin, 1964'''; US Stein and Day, 1965.
⚠️ '''Correction to a common statement: Comfort wrote the Introduction and Archer wrote the
Preface''', not the other way round.

'''Rights: IN COPYRIGHT.''' The copyright page reads verbatim: *"FIRST PUBLISHED IN 1964 …
This translation © Alex Comfort 1964. Preface © George Allen and Unwin Ltd, 1964."*
US: 1964 → renewal automatic → '''2060'''. UK: Comfort 1920–2000 → life+70 → '''2071'''.

⚠️ '''This is the catalogue's main legal exposure.''' A full, freely downloadable OCR scan
exists at `hnqa_the-koka-shastra-and-other-medieval-indian-writings-on-love-trans-by-alex-comfor`
'''tagged CC0 1.0 on Internet Archive'''. The uploader (Sarayu Foundation Trust / UP State
Museum Lucknow, under an IKS–MoE grant) '''has no authority to dedicate Allen & Unwin's or
Comfort's estate's rights.''' Do not rely on that tag. The correctly restricted
borrow-only copies are `kokashastrabeing00kokk` and `kokashastra0000unse`.

'''Is there a PD translation? No.''' No pre-1931 English ''Ratirahasya'' exists in Open
Library, Internet Archive, Wellcome or GRETIL. '''The nearest free route is again Richard
Schmidt's German''' — ''Beiträge zur indischen Erotik: das Liebesleben des Sanskritvolkes''
(Berlin: Barsdorf, '''1922'''; first Lotus-Verlag, Leipzig, 1902), which is '''Comfort's own
source''' for the later texts. '''PD in US (1922) and EU/UK (since 2010).''' Scans:
`beitrgezurindi00schm`, `in.ernet.dli.2015.134694`, `in.ernet.dli.2015.142227`.

'''Comfort 1964's exact scope, documented from the book's own OCR''' — it is the pivot
volume for five texts and it is worth knowing precisely what it does and does not contain:
full ''Ratirahasya'' (15 chapters); '''full ''Ratimañjarī''''' (pp. 88–95); '''exordium plus
synopsis only''' for ''Pañcasāyaka'' (81–83), ''Kandarpacūḍāmaṇi'' (83–84), ''Smaradīpikā''
(84–86), ''Anaṅgaraṅga'' (86–88) and ''Dīnālāpanikā Śukasaptati'' (95–98); and descriptive
treatment of ''Nāgarasarvasva'' and ''Ratiratnapradīpikā'' (98–103). Comfort states he
'''never obtained the ''Ratiratnapradīpikā'' text at all.'''

=== Nāgarasarvasva (attributed to Padmaśrī) ===

''Nāgarasarvasva'' / ''Nāgarakasarvasva'' ("Everything for the Man-About-Town"), 18
''paricchedas''. ⚠️ '''Date unsettled''' — commonly c. 10th–12th c.; no defensible date was
found in any source reached.

'''The author, Padmaśrī''' (colophons: ''Padmaśrījñāna''), is '''confirmed Buddhist''' — Comfort
notes it is the only erotic work in the corpus Mahāyāna in orientation, '''invoking
Mañjuśrī and Tārā rather than the Hindu patron deities.''' That makes it the most
interesting outlier on this shelf. Nothing biographical is known.

'''English translation: none documented, full or standalone.''' Comfort 1964 gives scattered
passages in footnotes plus a descriptive page (p. 98). The scholarship is:
'''Siegfried Lienhard, "Observations concerning a Buddhist text on erotics: the
Nāgarasarvasva of Padmaśrī," ''Central Asiatic Journal'' 23 (1979), 96–103'''
(<https://indianmedicine.eldoc.ub.rug.nl/25065/>); and '''Daud Ali, "Padmaśrī's
Nāgarasarvasva and the World of Medieval Kāmaśāstra," ''Journal of Indian Philosophy''
39/1 (2011), 41–62''', DOI 10.1007/s10781-010-9116-6 (paywalled). ⚠️ Ali has described his
work as "an extensive study and translation" — '''no published translation was located;
status unresolved.'''

'''Sanskrit editions, PD in US:''' 1921 (ed. Tanasukharāma Śarmā, Bombay — no scan found);
'''1929 Calcutta''' — <https://archive.org/details/Nagarasarvasva-of-Padmasri> (PDF,
Devanagari OCR); 1929 Hindi (Śrīveṅkaṭeśvara). The undated Rāmsāgar Tripāṭhī edition:
rights unsettled. A palm-leaf manuscript in Newari script (NAK 1/248, reel B 14/30) is
catalogued at Hamburg. '''Not on GRETIL.'''

=== Pañcasāyaka of Jyotirīśvara ===

''Pañcasāyaka'' ("The Five Arrows," after Kāmadeva's arrows), in five ''sāyakas''.
⚠️ '''Date disputed, 11th–14th c.''' — Schmidt says 11th; Comfort says the first half of the
'''14th''' ("next in age after the Koka Shastra"); Wellcome says 14th.

'''Author: Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara''', Maithili court poet — the same author as the
''Varṇaratnākara'' (Maithili prose) and the ''Dhūrtasamāgama'', confirmed by the Leipzig KOHD
colophon and GRETIL's author field. The text's own exordium names its sources: Vātsyāyana,
Goṇiputraka, Mūladeva, Bābhravya, Nandīśvara, Rantideva and Kṣemendra.

'''English translation: none complete.''' ⚠️ The Comfort claim must be stated precisely:
Comfort 1964 pp. '''81–83''' gives a translated '''exordium of about 200 words''' plus a
chapter-by-chapter synopsis — '''not the text'''. Comfort states the longer manuscripts
"have never been published," and that his own Pañcasāyaka material is '''second-hand from
Richard Schmidt'''. Substantial excerpts exist in '''German''' in Schmidt's ''Beiträge'' (1922,
PD).

'''Sanskrit:''' ★ '''1905, ed. Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya — PD in US, free scan at
<https://archive.org/details/pacasyaka00jyot>''' (Robarts/Toronto, Sanskrit only). Also
1925 (Wellcome) and 1928 Hindi, both PD US; the 1995 Kṛṣṇadāsa Akādamī edition is in
copyright. '''GRETIL e-text:''' `sa_jyotirIzvarakavizekhara-paJcasAyaka.xml`, input Dhaval
Patel — ⚠️ the TEI header says '''"(source unknown)"'''; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0.

=== Other texts in the genre ===

'''Kuṭṭanīmata of Dāmodaragupta.''' A ''nidarśanakāvya'' of ~1,058 verses — frame-narrative
satire. '''Late 8th c. CE, and among the most securely dated works in classical Sanskrit''':
Dāmodaragupta was minister to '''Jayāpīḍa''' of Kashmir (Kārkoṭa, r. c. 776–807), known from
Kalhaṇa's ''Rājataraṅgiṇī''.
* ★ '''PD English: E. Powys Mathers, ''Eastern Love'' Vol. I, "The Lessons of a Bawd,"'''
  London: John Rodker, '''1927'''. PD in US (1927) and UK/EU (Mathers 1892–1939, PD since
  2010). Scan: <https://archive.org/details/dli.venugopal.500>
* '''Csaba Dezső & Dominic Goodall, ''The Bawd's Counsel''''' (Groningen Oriental Studies 23,
  Egbert Forsten, '''2012''') — critical edition plus facing English translation from a
  previously unconsulted 13th-c. Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript. '''Fully in copyright.'''
* ★ '''GRETIL carries the Dezső–Goodall constituted Sanskrit text, contributed by the
  editors themselves''', under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0:
  `sa_dAmodaragupta-kuTTanImata.xml` (filed under Kāvya, not Kāmaśāstra). The best
  machine-readable witness and legitimately reusable non-commercially.
* Also PD: J. J. Meyer's German, Lotus-Verlag, Leipzig, '''1903'''; the 1924 Sanskrit ed.
* ⚠️ '''Verified negative: there is no Clay Sanskrit Library Kuṭṭanīmata.''' CSL's *Three
  Satires* is Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita, Kṣemendra and Bhallaṭa.

'''Samayamātṛkā of Kṣemendra.''' Eight ''samayas''; satire. '''11th c. CE, after 1037.'''
Kṣemendra (Vyāsadāsa) was a Kashmiri polymath and a '''pupil of Abhinavagupta''' — which
links this shelf directly to the Trika material in §1.5.
* ★ '''PD English: E. Powys Mathers, ''Eastern Love'' Vol. II, "The Harlot's Breviary,"'''
  Rodker 1927. PD US and UK/EU. Standalone upload with IA rights field '''Public Domain
  Mark 1.0''': <https://archive.org/details/SamayaMatrika>
* '''A. N. D. Haksar, ''The Courtesan's Keeper''''' (Rupa, 2008) — in copyright. ⚠️ A Penguin
  2011 reissue is cited by Wikipedia but unconfirmed.
* Sanskrit: Kāvyamālā No. 10, Nirṇaya Sāgar Press, 1925 reprint of the 1888 first —
  `in.ernet.dli.2015.283726`, IA rights "in Public Domain". '''Not on GRETIL.'''
* ⚠️ '''Verified negative: no CSL Samayamātṛkā''' (CSL's Kṣemendra satire is the
  ''Narmamālā'').

'''Ratimañjarī (attributed to Jayadeva).''' 125 ślokas. ⚠️ '''No secure date''' — Comfort calls
it "a lateish work," probably 15th–17th c. '''Attribution clarified from Comfort's own
text:''' *"it is not by 'the' Jayadeva, author of the Gīta Govinda, but more probably by one
Jayadeva the Encyclopaedist; or by some other Jayadeva, nobody can now say."*
'''Comfort 1964 pp. 88–95 is the first and apparently only complete English translation''' —
and therefore in copyright to 2060/2071. An earlier '''Italian''' version exists: S.
Pavolini, ''Giornale della Società Asiatica Italiana'' 17 (1904), p. 517 — PD, but ⚠️ '''no
scan URL located.'''

'''Smaradīpikā.''' ⚠️ '''More than one work bears this name''' — Comfort: "these poems, for
there appear to be more than one of the same name." '''Date unsettled'''; later than the
''Ratirahasya''. ⚠️ '''Authorship is unreconciled across four sources:''' the exordium names
'''Rudra'''; Comfort records "Kadra or Rudra or Garga"; GRETIL attributes it to
'''Mīnanātha'''; the 2004 Chowkhamba Hindi edition to '''Macchaghnapāda''' (a by-name of the
Nātha siddha Mīnanātha). Not resolved anywhere.
'''No complete English translation is documented''' (Comfort gives exordium and synopsis
only). ⚠️ '''No public-domain printed edition of the Smaradīpikā could be located at all''' —
the editions are 1967 and 2004 Chowkhamba, both in copyright. GRETIL's
`sa_mInanAtha-smaradIpikA.xml` is the only reliable digital text, and ⚠️ '''its source is
the in-copyright 1967 Chowkhamba edition''', hosted under GRETIL's remove-on-claim
disclaimer. Flag the tension.

'''Kandarpacūḍāmaṇi of Vīrabhadradeva.''' '''Early 16th c.''', credited to '''Vīrabhadra(deva),
King of Rewa''' (Vāghelā). ⚠️ One IA record dates it 1626 — unreconciled, likely a Vikrama
Saṃvat date (= 1569 CE) or a copying date. '''Comfort's judgement from the exordium is that
Vīrabhadra was the patron, not the author''': "It looks like the work of a court poet, who
must have been a ghost commissioned by 'godlike King Virabhadra'."
Genre matters here: it is a technically skilful, '''very close verse recasting of
Vātsyāyana's prose Kāmasūtra into Āryā metre''' (Comfort's analogy: the Scottish Metrical
Psalter). Because of that, '''any Kāmasūtra translation is a close content proxy''', which
makes the absence of an English translation much less costly than it looks.
Sanskrit editions PD in US: 1924 (ed. Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya, Bombay) and 1926 (ed.
Rāmacandra Śāstrī, Lahore), both on Internet Archive. '''Not on GRETIL.'''

'''The Jayamaṅgalā in English.''' '''No standalone English translation exists.''' It has only
ever appeared '''embedded in''' Kāmasūtra translations: Burton 1883 (absorbed silently, not
presented as a translated text); '''Daniélou 1994 — full and interleaved''', the closest
thing to an English Jayamaṅgalā, and in copyright; Doniger & Kakar 2002 — '''selected'''
passages in notes. '''The one complete Western-language Jayamaṅgalā is Schmidt's German,
and it is public domain everywhere.'''

'''Rasamañjarī of Bhānudatta''' (rasa and ''nāyikā'' typology — adjacent, not erotology
proper). English: '''Sheldon Pollock, ''"Bouquet of Rasa" & "River of Rasa"'', Clay Sanskrit
Library, NYU Press, 2009 — in copyright.''' PD Sanskrit editions: 1904, 1929.

'''Ratiratnapradīpikā of Prauḍha Devarāja''' (15th c.). ⚠️ '''Nothing located''' — no Open
Library record, no scan, no translation. Comfort admits he never obtained the text.
'''Unsettled.'''

'''Named but with no English translation found for any:''' ''Kuchumāra Tantra'',
''Manasollāsa / Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi'' (Someśvara III), ''Janavaśya'' (Kallarasa),
''Dattakasūtra'', ''Ratikallolinī'' (Dīkṣita Samarāja), ''Śṛṅgāradīpikā'' (Harihara),
''Śṛṅgārarasaprabandhadīpikā'' (Kumāra Harihara), ''Smarapradīpikā'' (Guṇākara),
''Kāmasamūha'' of Ananta (15th c.) — plus the '''lost early authorities''' the tradition
itself cites: Nandi/Nandikeśvara, Bābhravya, Cārāyaṇa, Gonikāputra, Dattaka, Suvarṇanābha,
Ghoṭakamukha, Gonardīya, and Kṣemendra's lost ''Vātsyāyanasūtrasāra''.

=== ★ The E. Powys Mathers "Eastern Love" set — the one PD English route into this corpus ===
'''Twelve volumes, London: John Rodker, "for subscribers," 1927–1930'''; a US three-volume
edition from Horace Liveright, New York, 1930. '''Every volume is now PD in both the US and
the UK''' — vols. I–XI (1927–29) and vol. XII (1930 → US PD since 1 Jan 2026); Mathers
1892–1939 → UK/EU PD since 2010. Vol. I is the ''Kuṭṭanīmata'', Vol. II the ''Samayamātṛkā''.

⚠️ '''Scholarly caveat, and it is a real one:''' Mathers's works "are not scholarly works,
and are in some cases based on intermediate versions in European languages." Treat these
as '''free literary renderings, in places made via French — not translations from
Sanskrit.''' They are usable precisely because they are free, and they must be labelled
for what they are.

== 1.4 Greek and Roman ==

The Greco-Roman amatory corpus is the '''best-cleared''' shelf in this catalogue. Nearly
everything of importance has a public-domain English translation, several have more than
one, and Project Gutenberg, Perseus and Internet Archive hold open full texts. The
Victorian privately-printed translations — Burton, Smithers and their circle — are all
clear in both the US and the UK, because Burton died in 1890 and Smithers in 1907.

The characteristic rights trap on this shelf is not the translation but the '''revision''':
Loeb volumes are routinely reissued with a modern reviser's name added, and the revision
is a new copyrighted work. Mozley's 1929 Ovid is free; Goold's 1979 revision of it is
not. Ker's 1919–20 Martial is free; Shackleton Bailey's 1993 revision is not.

=== Ovid — ''Ars Amatoria'' and ''Remedia Amoris'' ===
Latin, elegiac couplets. ''Ars amatoria'' in three books, c. 1 BCE – 2 CE; ''Remedia amoris'',
one book, c. 2 CE. Publius Ovidius Naso, 43 BCE – 17/18 CE.

'''The exile.''' Ovid was relegated to Tomis in '''8 CE''' — ''relegatio'', not ''exilium'': he kept
property and citizenship and there was no senatorial decree. At ''Tristia'' 2.207 he names
two causes, ''"carmen et error"'' — a poem and a mistake. The '''carmen''' is near-universally
identified as the ''Ars Amatoria'', written some seven years earlier and out of step with
the Augustan moral legislation (the ''lex Iulia'' programme of c. 18 BCE). The '''error''' is
never specified and has never been identified; the Julia-scandal theory is speculation.
Philip Hardie's reading — that the ''error'' supplied the '''pretext''' in 8 CE for a late
retaliatory blow against the poem — is the sober one. Rome's city council passed a
symbolic motion revoking the banishment in December 2017.

|-

'''Perseus''' carries the ''Ars'' in Latin (Ehwald, `urn:cts:latinLit:phi0959.phi004.perseus-lat1`)
and in English as the '''Dryden/Congreve''' version of the 1709 Garth circle
(`...opp-eng1`, `...perseus-eng1`) — '''not''' Riley or Mozley. All PD.

'''Not free:''' Peter Green (Penguin, 1982); Rolfe Humphries (Indiana UP, 1957);
A. D. Melville (Oxford, 1990); Goold's 1979 Loeb revision.

=== The ''Priapeia'' ===
Eighty short anonymous Latin poems, 1st or early 2nd c. CE.

'''Authorship.''' The traditional view is an anthology by many hands. Since '''Vinzenz
Buchheit's 1962 study''' the single-author view has gained ground: the metres fall into
five groups of fourteen, consecutive poems are linked by repeated words, the sequence
forms a quasi-biography of the god, and the second dedicatory poem has the poet claim to
have ''written'' rather than ''collected'' them. Four anonymous Priapic poems from the
''Appendix Vergiliana'' appear as nos. 84, 86, 87 and 88 in the English edition.

'''The 1890 English translation.''' ''Priapeia, sive diversorum poetarum in Priapum lusus'',
"Cosmopoli, 1890," printed for the '''Erotika Biblion Society''' of London for private
subscribers; 95 poems. The title page is pseudonymous — verse by "Outidanos," notes and
excursus by "Neaniskos." The standard attribution is '''Richard Burton''' (verse) and
'''Leonard C. Smithers''' (prose and notes); sacred-texts' own editorial note holds that
Burton's authorship of the notes can be established despite the introduction's disclaimer.
⚠️ The Outidanos/Neaniskos identifications rest on '''trade bibliography''' (antiquarian
booksellers), not on independently verified scholarship — treat as probable, not settled.

* '''Full text:''' <https://sacred-texts.com/cla/priap/index.htm>. ⚠️ '''Important caveat the
  site states itself:''' the file is a '''merge''' — the Smithers–Burton copies available
  lacked the Latin, so a Latin text from elsewhere was merged in. It is '''not''' a faithful
  transcription of a single 1890 copy.
* ⚠️ sacred-texts.com returns HTTP 403 to automated fetches; the URL is correct in a
  browser.
* No open Internet Archive scan of the 1890 edition itself was located. The Latin
  tradition is abundantly scanned and PD (Noël's 1798 ''Erotopaegnion'' is '''Gutenberg
  #53944'''; Mooney's 1916 ''Minor Poems of Vergil'' carries the Appendix Vergiliana Priapea
  in English).
* '''Rights:''' the 1890 translation is '''PD in the US and UK'''.
* '''Not free:''' W. H. Parker (1988); Richard W. Hooper (1999); Kytzler (1978, German).

=== Martial — ''Epigrammata'' ===
Over 1,500 Latin epigrams in twelve books plus the ''Liber spectaculorum'', ''Xenia'' and
''Apophoreta'', published 86–103 CE. Marcus Valerius Martialis, c. 38/41 – c. 102/104 CE.

'''The bowdlerising quirk, which is a genuinely interesting bibliographic fact.''' In
'''Bohn's Classical Library (1897, George Bell & Sons; translator anonymous)''', the
translator left the obscene epigrams '''untranslated in the Latin and printed an existing
Italian translation alongside them'''. This is the Victorian form of a convention the Loeb
series then inherited: '''Greek judged too ribald was rendered into Latin, and Latin judged
too ribald into Italian''' — the obscenity preserved intact, but behind a language barrier
the schoolroom reader could not cross. Over 400 of Martial's epigrams were held unfit for
school use. Ker's Loeb is euphemistic rather than non-translating; the restored
unexpurgated text is '''Shackleton Bailey's 1993 Loeb, fully in copyright'''.

* '''Project Gutenberg has essentially nothing.''' There is '''no PG edition of Martial's
  Epigrams''' — a real gap in the free web corpus, worth noting.
* '''tertullian.org''' (Roger Pearse, 2008, rev. 2010), Bohn-based and modernised:
  <https://tertullian.org/fathers/martial_epigrams_00eintro.htm> — the page states
  explicitly '''"This file and all material on this page is in the public domain - copy
  freely."''' Expurgated as described.
* '''Internet Archive, Bohn (open, PD):''' `epigramsmartial00bohngoog` (1897),
  `epigramsmartial01bohngoog` (1877), `epigrams00mart` (1860).
* '''Internet Archive, Ker's Loeb (open, PD):''' `epigramswithengl02martuoft` (1920),
  `epigrams00kergoog` (1919), `martialepigrams01martiala`/`02martiala` (1919).
  '''PD in US (1919–20); UK PD since 2000 (Ker d. 1929).''' Clean on both sides.
* '''UNSETTLED / in copyright:''' 1925, 1961 and 1968 printings; Shackleton Bailey 1993.

=== The Greek Anthology — Books V and XII ===
Greek epigrams spanning the 7th c. BCE to the 10th c. CE. Meleager of Gadara's ''Garland''
(c. 60 BCE) → Philippus → Agathias → '''Constantine Cephalas's 10th-c. recension in
fifteen books''', surviving in a single manuscript, the '''Codex Palatinus''' (Heidelberg).
'''Maximus Planudes''' (c. 1301–1320) made a shortened seven-book recension and
'''bowdlerised''' much of what he thought too explicit; the Planudean was the only version
known in the West until '''1606''', when Salmasius copied the Palatine. Brunck printed the
Palatine in 1776. The manuscript was split after the 1623 sack of Heidelberg, reached
Paris in 1797 and returned incomplete in 1816.

* '''Book V''' = the amatory epigrams. '''Book XII''' = '''Strato of Sardis's ''Musa Puerilis''''',
  the homoerotic book.

'''⚠️ A correction worth recording.''' It is often said that '''W. R. Paton rendered Book XII
into Latin''' rather than English in his Loeb. '''This was checked against the text and it
is false.''' Paton's Book XII appears in '''English throughout, 12.1 to 12.258'''. Paton
translated the ''Musa Puerilis'' into English, which is itself historically notable and is
why the Loeb was for decades the only accessible complete English Book XII. The
Latin-veil practice is real and well attested — but the documented cases are '''Edmonds's
Loeb Longus''', '''Heseltine's 1913 Loeb Petronius''' (whose preface admits leaving whole
pages "in the decent obscurity of a learned language"), and '''the Bohn Martial'''
(Latin → Italian). Some early Loebs also '''reversed the gender of the beloved'''. Attribute
the practice to those, not to Paton.

'''Paton's Loeb.''' ''The Greek Anthology'', 5 vols, Heinemann/Putnam, '''1916–1918''' (Loeb
67, 68, 84, 85, 86). Vol. I = Books 1–6 (incl. '''Book V'''); '''Vol. IV = Books 10–12'''
(incl. '''Book XII'''). Paton d. 1921 → '''PD in US; UK PD since 1992.'''
* Open Internet Archive scans: `in.ernet.dli.2015.103642` (vol. 4, 1916 — the Book XII
  volume; archive.org metadata reads "NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT"); `in.ernet.dli.2015.529388`
  (vol. 1, Book V); `greekanthology03pato`; `greekanthologyin0005wrtr`.
* '''Free full text online:''' <https://topostext.org/work/535> (Books 10–12, Paton 1916).
* ⚠️ Borrow-only / UNSETTLED: the 1939, 1948 and 1969 printings.

'''Earlier and other PD versions.''' '''George Burges''', Bohn's Classical Library, '''1854'''
(the title — ''as selected for the use of Westminster, Eton, and other public schools'' —
declares its expurgatory purpose); open scans `greekanthology0000geor`,
`greekanthologya04burggoog`. Paton's '''separate''' pre-Loeb *Anthologiae Graecae Erotica:
The Love Epigrams, or Book V of the Palatine Anthology* (Nutt, '''1898''') is a distinct
Book-V-only edition, PD. '''Gutenberg's only substantial holding is #2378''', J. W. Mackail,
''Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology'' (1890, rev. 1906) — PD in US; UK PD since 2016.
'''No Gutenberg edition of the complete Anthology exists.'''

'''Not free:''' Peter Jay (Penguin, 1973/81); '''Daryl Hine, ''Puerilities''''' (Princeton, 2001 —
the standard modern Book XII); the 2014–16 Loeb revisions.

=== Burton's "Terminal Essay" and the "Sotadic Zone" — a document in the history of the scholarship ===
In '''Volume 10''', the final volume of Burton's ''Book of the Thousand Nights and a Night'',
"Benares: Kamashastra Society, for private subscribers only," '''1885–86''' (the Benares
imprint is fictitious; it was printed in Stoke Newington). The "Sotadic Zone" is in the
Terminal Essay's '''Section IV, Part D'''. Burton posited a geographic-climatic belt — the
Mediterranean, North Africa, the Levant, much of the Middle East and Asia, and the whole
of the Americas — in which he claimed pederasty was endemic; the name derives from
'''Sotades''', 3rd-c. BCE Greek poet.

* '''Gutenberg #3444''' (vol. 10) — <https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3444> — PD in the USA;
  a second independent PG transcription is '''#58360'''. Internet Archive
  `in.ernet.dli.2015.499370` (open). '''PD worldwide''' (Burton d. 1890).
* ⚠️ '''burtoniana.org, which is widely cited as hosting it, returned HTTP 403 and was not
  verified. Do not publish that URL untested.'''
* ⚠️ Internet Archive items `bookofthousandni10burtuoft` and `...11burtuoft` belong to the
  '''1894 Nichols/Smithers twelve-volume "Library Edition"''', where volume numbering
  differs — check the title page before citing a volume number.

'''Its present standing, stated honestly, because the catalogue has to.''' The Terminal Essay
is '''historically important and thoroughly discredited'''. It is read in two literatures:
the history of sexology, as the first extended English ethnographic treatment of male
homosexuality, alongside Symonds's ''A Problem in Greek Ethics'' (privately printed 1883;
PD, sacred-texts `/lgbt/pge/`) and Ellis–Symonds's ''Sexual Inversion'' (1897); and
Orientalism critique — Said's ''Orientalism'' (1978), Rana Kabbani's *Europe's Myths of
Orient* (1986), and '''Joseph Allen Boone's ''The Homoerotics of Orientalism''''' (Columbia,
2014), which reads the Sotadic Zone as projecting European sexual anxiety onto a mapped
elsewhere. The climatic determinism is rejected outright and the ethnography is anecdotal
and second-hand. It is cited today as a '''primary source about Victorian sexual-imperial
thought''', essentially never as evidence about the societies it describes. Any use of
Burton in this corpus — and he is unavoidable, since he is also the Kama Sutra, the
Ananga Ranga and the Perfumed Garden — should carry that framing.

---

== 1.5 Tantra — the distinction, stated accurately ==

This section matters more than its length suggests. The operator's own ecosystem is
'''Shaivite''', and the single most common error in this subject area is to present the
modern Western sexual-practice synthesis as though it were the Shaiva and Shakta
scriptural tradition. They are different things with different histories, and the
catalogue says which is which.

=== (i) The actual textual tradition ===
The Sanskrit tantric/āgamic corpus is a '''revealed scriptural literature of initiatory
ritual''', overwhelmingly Śaiva and Śākta on the Hindu side, with parallel Vaiṣṇava
Pāñcarātra and Buddhist Vajrayāna corpora. Composed roughly '''5th–13th c. CE''', with
exegesis continuing later. The principal streams:

* '''Śaiva Siddhānta''' — the dualist, ritually normative mainstream. Its canon is
  traditionally held to contain twenty-eight scriptures, '''but the lists vary''', and
  several doctrinally central texts (the ''Mṛgendra'', for instance) are not on them. A
  Sanskrit scriptural layer plus a Tamil devotional and philosophical layer (''Tirumurai'',
  the Meykaṇḍa śāstras). Exegetes: Sadyojyoti (c. 7th c.), Bhoja (''Tattvaprakāśa'',
  c. 1018), Somaśambhu, Aghoraśiva.
* '''Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism — Trika and Pratyabhijñā''' — Vasugupta, Somānanda,
  Utpaladeva, '''Abhinavagupta (c. 950–1016)''' and his pupil Kṣemarāja; the
  ''Mālinīvijayottara'' as the Trika's root scripture; the '''Tantrāloka''' as its summa.
* '''Kaula and Kāpālika streams''' — the transgressive, cremation-ground strata from which
  the kaula lineages (Matsyendranātha, the Yoginī-kaula) emerge. The '''Nātha''' tradition
  is continuous with this. This connects directly to
  `Pashupata_Shaivism.wiki`, which already takes the correct line that the later Trika and
  Nātha orders ''domesticate'' what the earlier ascetic orders did.

=== The proportion question, answered as precisely as the sources allow ===
'''Sexual ritual is a small minority of the tantric scriptural corpus by volume, and is
restricted within it.''' The overwhelming bulk is initiation (''dīkṣā''), daily and occasional
ritual, mantra-śāstra, mandala construction, iconography, temple and image installation,
yoga and subtle-body physiology, cosmology and the ''tattva'' ontology, apotropaic magic,
and funerary and expiatory procedure.

The qualitative support is strong: '''Teun Goudriaan's''' practice inventory (mantras,
mandalas, gestures, meditation, ritual worship, initiation) does not emphasise sex;
'''Georg Feuerstein's''' topic list has "sacred sexuality" as one item among many;
'''Gavin Flood's''' focus is the body in philosophy, ritual and art; '''Richard Payne''' states
flatly that Tantra "has been commonly but incorrectly associated with sex."

The best '''checkable''' illustration is structural. The '''Mahānirvāṇa Tantra''''s fourteen
chapters cover: questions on liberation; worship of Brahman; worship of Prakṛti; mantra
formation, jar-placing and elemental purification; śrī-pātra, homa and cakra; stotra and
kavaca '''and the kula-tattva (ch. 7)'''; caste and āśrama dharma; the ten saṃskāras;
śrāddha and funerary rites; expiatory rites; eternal dharma; installation of the devatā;
consecration of the śiva-liṅga; the four classes of avadhūtas. '''One chapter of fourteen
touches the pañcatattva. The rest is ritual, mantra, dharma and life-cycle rite.'''

⚠️ '''No scholar states an explicit percentage, and this document does not invent one.''' The
claim is well-supported qualitatively by Padoux, Payne, Goudriaan and Flood; it is '''not
reducible to a number.'''

=== The scholarly disagreement, represented rather than flattened ===
'''David Gordon White''', ''Kiss of the Yogini: "Tantric Sex" in its South Asian Contexts''
(Chicago, 2003), argues the opposite emphasis: that '''sexualised ritual is historically
primary in the earliest kaula strata''', not a late accretion, and that the "high"
philosophical Tantra of Abhinavagupta is a later semanticisation of an originally
concrete, fluid-based practice. White also argues that Tantra, not Bhakti or Vedānta, was
the South Asian mainstream from the 7th century to the modern period — and separately
insists that '''"tantrism" is "a 19th-century European invention not present in any Asian
language."'''

'''Gerald James Larson''', reviewing in the ''Journal of the American Oriental Society''
(2008), praises the book but rejects the mainstream thesis — White escapes the "Bhakti was
mainstream" trap only to fall into a new one — and holds that tantric sexuality was
'''largely allegorical and initiate-restricted'''. '''André Padoux''' and '''Christopher
Wallis''' represent the other pole: the corpus read whole is a ritual-philosophical system
in which sexual rite is one restricted element. Padoux: Tantrism is '''"a Western term and
notion, not a category that is used by Tantrikas themselves"''' — a formulation echoed by
C. Mackenzie Brown ("an apologetic label of Westerners") and David Gray ("a neologism of
western scholars").

'''The correct framing:''' the disagreement is about '''the earliest kaula strata and about
centrality''', not about whether the bulk of the ''surviving corpus by volume'' is ritual,
mantra and yoga — on that, White does not dissent. '''Both poles agree that modern
neo-Tantra misdescribes the tradition.'''

*(⚠️ Note on a common miscitation: James Mallinson's "The Yogīs' Latest Trick" (2013)
targets White's* Sinister Yogis*, not* Kiss of the Yogini.)

=== (ii) The neo-Tantra genealogy ===
This is a '''modern Western synthesis with a traceable lineage''', not a transmission.

{| class="wikitable"
! Figure / work !! Dates !! What is actually established

Kathleen Taylor (2001) links the "Avalon" pseudonym to Burne-Jones's ''Arthur's Sleep in Avalon'' and notes that '''Theosophists would have read such a name as signalling occult interests'''. He depended on a circle of Bengali pandit mentors, '''especially A. B. Ghose'''. The load-bearing point: he '''simultaneously made the texts available in English and framed them apologetically''' — presenting Tantra as respectable, Vedanta-compatible religion against colonial and missionary contempt. The Avalon corpus is both the foundation of Western textual access '''and''' the origin of a distorting lens. ⚠️ The extent of Ghose's authorship is a live scholarly question — use Taylor 2001 directly, do not state it flatly.

'''How neo-Tantra actually differs.''' It draws on Hindu and Buddhist tantras but
'''emphasises their sexual elements''', uses "tantra" as a catch-all for sacred sexuality,
admits unorthodox practices, and '''omits central parts of Indian tantric practice — in
particular the reliance on a guru.'''

'''And one nuance worth keeping, because flat debunking is its own inaccuracy.'''
'''Hugh Urban's''' own position is not simple dismissal: he reports the standard scholarly
criticism of "California Tantra" as "based on a profound misunderstanding of the Tantric
path," but calls it himself '''"simply a different interpretation for a specific historical
situation"''' — a legitimate object of study in the history of religions rather than merely
an error. '''Feuerstein''' is the harsher voice; '''Geoffrey Samuel''' argues modern Western
Tantra deserves more than dismissal.

'''The scholarship (all in copyright — cite, never reproduce):''' Hugh B. Urban, *Tantra:
Sex, Secrecy, Politics, and Power* (California, 2003) and ''Magia Sexualis'' (2006);
David Gordon White, ''Kiss of the Yogini'' (Chicago, 2003), ''The Alchemical Body'' (1996),
''Tantra in Practice'' (Princeton, 2000); Christopher D. Wallis, ''Tantra Illuminated''
(2012/2013); André Padoux, ''The Hindu Tantric World'' (Chicago, 2017) and ''Vāc'' (SUNY,
1990); '''Alexis Sanderson, "The Śaiva Age"''' in Einoo (ed.), *Genesis and Development of
Tantrism* (Tokyo, 2009) — the single most important survey of the historical spread of
Śaivism (⚠️ widely available as a free PDF, but '''both alexissanderson.com and the
University of Tokyo repository failed during verification — do not publish a URL
untested'''); Agehananda Bharati, ''The Tantric Tradition'' (1965), the earlier-generation
insider-scholar account.

=== (iii) The actual Tantric texts, with rights ===

'''Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra.''' Sanskrit, '''163 anuṣṭubh verses''', a dialogue between
Bhairava and Bhairavī; a Kaula-Trika Śaiva tantra, dated by Jaideva Singh tentatively to
the '''7th–8th c. CE'''. Abhinavagupta calls it the ''Śiva-jñāna-upaniṣad''. Commentaries by
'''Kṣemarāja''' (partial) and '''Śivopādhyāya''' (''Vivṛti''), published in the '''Kashmir Series
of Texts and Studies, 1918'''.
* '''PD Sanskrit:''' Internet Archive `in.ernet.dli.2015.242331` — the 1918 KSTS edition.
  '''PD.'''
* '''⚠️ KEY FINDING: there is NO public-domain English translation of the Vijñāna
  Bhairava.''' The earliest English rendering of any kind is '''Paul Reps, 1957'''
  ("Centering," a partial poetic version of the 112 dhāraṇās in ''Zen Flesh, Zen Bones'') —
  '''UNSETTLED, presumed in copyright'''; the 1957 US publication is renewal-dependent, the
  renewal database could not be reached, and Tuttle/Penguin keep it in print with a
  "© 1957, 1985" notice consistent with renewal. '''Treat as in copyright.''' Everything
  else is later: '''Lilian Silburn''''s French (1961, in copyright to 2064); '''Jaideva
  Singh''' (Motilal Banarsidass, 1979 — the standard scholarly English, in copyright);
  Lakshman Joo (2002); Satyasangananda Saraswati (2003); Semenov (2010); Lorin Roche's
  ''Radiance Sutras'' (2014, a free rendering); Osho (1998/2010); Wallis (2018).
* ⚠️ A full-text Jaideva Singh upload exists on Internet Archive. '''It is an infringing
  copy. Do not treat it as a rights source.'''
* '''Practical conclusion: for the VBT you can host the 1918 Sanskrit freely and nothing
  else. Any English must be licensed, or newly made from the PD Sanskrit.'''

'''Kaulajñānanirṇaya''' (of Matsyendranātha). The foundational Yoginī-Kaula scripture,
surviving in Nepalese manuscripts, conventionally '''9th–11th c. CE'''.
* '''P. C. Bagchi's edition''', *Kaulajñāna-nirṇaya and Some Minor Texts of the School of

  '''Bagchi's editorial apparatus and English summaries are a separate copyrightable

* '''⚠️ Magee's site, shivashakti.com, is a superb finding aid and a terrible rights

'''Kulārṇava Tantra.''' A late Kaula scripture in 17 ''ullāsas'', conventionally c. 11th–15th

* '''The PD edition:''' Tantrik Texts series Vol. V, Sanskrit text ed. '''Tārānātha

'''Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.''' ⚠️ '''Important for accuracy: this is a very late text''' — most

'''PART 2 — THE BRIDGE MAP'''

The classical erotological corpus is not a free-standing shelf. Almost every one of these
texts spends a substantial fraction of its length on '''materials''': unguents, perfumes,
powders, oils, pastes, medicated wines, foods. Vatsyayana's Book VII (''Aupanishadika''),
the ''Ananga Ranga'''s final chapters, the ''Perfumed Garden'''s recipe sections and the
Chinese bedchamber literature's dietetics are all, read flatly, '''formulary literature'''.
That is the actual seam with the Library — not the sexual content, the '''pharmacy'''.

This map names the article each bridge lands on, states what the classical text claims,
states what modern chemistry or physiology says, and separates the places where the two
genuinely meet from the places where the connection is only rhetorical. The three-tier
separation (established / preclinical / hypothesis-and-tradition) is house style and is
followed here.

---

== 2.1 The oils and aromatics shelf ==

=== Bridge A — Anointing oils and transdermal penetration enhancement ===
'''Lands on:''' `Balm_of_Gilead_and_Uziza.wiki` §3 "The Pharmacological Bridge: Resins,
Pungency, and Transdermal Driving"; `Punic_Wax.wiki` §"Amphiphilic Emulsification and
Transdermal Delivery"; `Head_Cone.wiki`; `Kyphi.wiki`.

'''What the classical texts claim.''' The Sanskrit, Arabic and Greco-Roman erotological
texts all prescribe compounded '''anointing preparations''' — a resin or fat base carrying
aromatics and pungent spices — applied to skin, and they attribute effects to the
application that go beyond scent and lubrication. The ''Perfumed Garden'''s recipe
sections and ''Kama Sutra'' VII are the densest examples; Ovid's *Medicamina Faciei
Femineae* is the Roman parallel for the cosmetic side of the same practice.

'''What the modern science says.''' This is the '''strongest''' bridge in the whole map,
because the mechanism the ancient formularies implicitly exploit is real and the Library
already documents it. The stratum corneum is a ceramide/cholesterol/free-fatty-acid
lamellar barrier. Monoterpenes and sesquiterpenes (β-caryophyllene, the pinenes,
1,8-cineole, d-limonene) and ''Piperaceae'' alkylamides (piperine, guineensine)
'''fluidise that lipid matrix''' and function as penetration accelerators — this is
established pharmaceutics, not folklore, and it is why terpenes appear in modern
transdermal patch formulations. A resin-plus-pungent-spice unguent is, in mechanism, a
penetration-enhanced topical.

'''Where they genuinely meet:''' the ''structure'' of the preparations. A heavy
non-volatile base (wax, fat, resin) plus a volatile penetration-enhancing fraction is the
same architecture as a modern transdermal vehicle. The ancient formularies arrived at it
empirically.

'''Where it is only rhetorical:''' the ''claimed endpoint''. Enhanced penetration of an
anti-inflammatory resin is established. Enhanced penetration producing a specific
sexual-pharmacological effect is '''not''' demonstrated for any of these preparations, and
no classical formula has been tested as such. The mechanism is real; the advertised
outcome is unvalidated.

=== Bridge B — Perfumery as one of the sixty-four arts ===
'''Lands on:''' `Aroma_Wheels_Euphoric_Odours_and_the_Science_of_Aromatherapy.wiki`;
`Standardized_Extracts_Enhanced_Leaf_and_the_Perfumery_of_Botanical_Aroma.wiki`;
`Hydrosols_Absolutes_and_Botanical_Extraction_Modalities.wiki`.

'''What the classical text claims.''' Vatsyayana's ''chatuḥṣaṣṭi kalā'' — the sixty-four
arts a cultivated person was expected to hold — include '''perfume compounding'''
(''gandhayukti''), garland-making, cosmetics, cooking, and the preparation of scented
waters. Erotology in the Sanskrit tradition is explicitly presented as a branch of
''civility'', and perfumery is one of its named technical skills. The Arabic tradition is
named for the practice: ''al-Rawd al-'Atir'' is "the perfumed/scented garden."

'''What the modern science says.''' The Library's aroma shelf is the direct modern
continuation of this craft, and it already does the honest work of separating the three
things that get called "the effect of a smell." The relevant finding from
`Scent_as_a_Drug_Route...` is the '''six-to-nine orders of magnitude''' gap between
olfactory detection (picogram–nanogram) and receptor-level pharmacology (needs
milligrams absorbed).

'''Where they genuinely meet:''' the classical texts treat scent as a '''social and
affective technology''', not as a drug — and on the Library's own three-way split, that is
mechanism (3), learned and cultural association, which is ''real and powerful'' and simply
not pharmacology. The ancient authors are, on this point, more accurate than modern
aromatherapy marketing.

'''Where it is only rhetorical:''' any reading that upgrades a classical perfume recipe to
a pharmacological aphrodisiac. The Library's own dose argument forbids it.

=== Bridge C — Jasmine, indole, and the specific euphoric-odour claim ===
'''Lands on:''' `Scent_as_a_Drug_Route_Volatile_Indoles_Jasmine_and_the_Olfactory_Path.wiki`;
`A_Field_Guide_to_Smell_Molecules...wiki` §4 and §7.

Jasmine, sandalwood, musk, saffron, costus and aloeswood are the recurring aromatics
across the Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian texts. The Library's existing treatment is the
right one to hang this on: the '''GABA-A potentiation''' finding (Aoshima & Hamamoto 1999)
for benzyl acetate and related floral esters is documented ''in vitro''; the inhaled-linalool
anxiolytic result (Linck et al. 2010) with the anosmic-mouse control (Kashiwadani et al.
2018) is the strongest mechanistic result in the field — and it establishes that the
effect runs '''through the nose as a smell''', not by blood absorption. Classical texts
calling jasmine relaxing are describing something real with the wrong causal story.

=== Bridge D — The citrus furanocoumarins: one molecule family, two different harms ===
'''Lands on:''' `Cytochrome_P450_System_Inhibition_and_Induction.wiki` (bergamottin,
6',7'-dihydroxybergamottin, mechanism-based inactivation, 48–72 h recovery);
`Bioavailability_Metabolic_Inhibition_and_Synergy.wiki` §3; `A_Field_Guide_to_Smell_
Molecules...wiki` §14 (bergapten/5-MOP phototoxicity, FCF bergamot);
`Cold_Pressing_Expelling_and_Heat_Why_the_Same_Seed_Gives_Different_Oils.wiki`
(why ''expressed'' citrus oils carry furocoumarins and distilled ones do not).

This is the '''most load-bearing safety bridge''' and it belongs to Part 3 as much as Part 2.
The Library already carries the oral story: grapefruit furanocoumarins irreversibly
inactivate enterocyte CYP3A4. The adult-surface material needs the ''dermal'' story, which
is a '''different mechanism with the same molecule class''': bergapten (5-methoxypsoralen)
is a psoralen; under UVA it intercalates DNA and forms interstrand crosslinks, producing
phytophotodermatitis — a real chemical burn, not an irritation. Two harms, two
mechanisms, one compound family. Conflating them would be exactly the error the Library's
house style exists to prevent. See §3.5.

=== Bridge E — Extraction method determines the hazard ===
'''Lands on:''' `Terpene_Extraction.wiki`; `Cold_Pressing_Expelling_and_Heat...wiki`;

Practical, and under-appreciated: '''cold-expressed''' citrus peel oil carries

non-volatile and stay behind. The same plant yields a phototoxic and a non-phototoxic
oil depending only on the method. The Library already states this; the adult surface
needs it stated again at the point of use, because "lime oil" on a label means nothing
without the method.

=== Bridge F — Book VII and the aphrodisiac formularies ===
'''Lands on:''' `Oilahuasca.wiki`; `Cooking_with_Herbs_and_Spices.wiki`;
`Tinctures_Glycerites_Syrups_and_Infused_Oils_and_Butters.wiki`;
`Spiced_Wine_Bitters_and_the_Colas.wiki`.

'''What the classical texts claim.''' Vatsyayana VII, the ''Ananga Ranga'''s closing
chapters, and the ''Perfumed Garden'' all carry '''aphrodisiac and "subjugation" recipes''' —
medicated ghees, honeys, milks, spiced wines, powders. Many are frankly magical
(sympathetic-magic ingredients, incantations); many are ordinary kitchen pharmacy: long
pepper, black pepper, ginger, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, saffron, sesame, ghee, honey,
milk, asparagus (''shatavari''), ''Mucuna''.

'''What the modern science says.''' The Library's framework handles this cleanly and
should be the lens:
* '''Mechanistically real and already documented here:''' piperine as a CYP and UGT
  inhibitor and bioavailability enhancer; nutmeg and cinnamon as allylbenzene sources
  within the Oilahuasca/Oswald-pathway material; ''Mucuna pruriens'' as a genuine L-DOPA
  source (this is the one unambiguously pharmacologically active aphrodisiac-adjacent
  botanical in the Sanskrit lists, and it is dopaminergic, which is a real mechanism for
  libido).
* '''Preclinical at best:''' ''Tribulus'', ''shatavari'', most of the "rasayana" claims.
* '''Tradition only:''' the sympathetic-magic recipes, which the texts themselves often
  frame as such.

'''Where they genuinely meet:''' the formularies are a '''historical ethnobotanical record'''
of which plants were believed to do this, and several of those plants turn out to have
real pharmacology — just usually ''not'' the pharmacology claimed. Nutmeg is psychoactive;
it is not an aphrodisiac. Long pepper is a potentiator; it is not a libido drug.

'''Where it is only rhetorical:''' treating Book VII as a working formulary. It is not. The
honest frame is: *these are the plants the tradition named, here is what each one
actually does, and the overlap with the claim is small.* Several of the named materials
are '''outright dangerous''' at the doses implied (nutmeg's anticholinergic delirium;
datura and ''Strychnos'' appear in some Indic and Arabic recipe traditions) and that
belongs on the page at the point the plant is named.
