'''PART 3 — WAX, OILS AND THE SAFETY MATERIAL'''

Written the way the Library writes harm reduction. The practical detail '''is''' the
material: a person who is going to do this and is told only "be careful" has been given
nothing, and withholding the numbers is the harm the library exists to prevent. The
numbers below are given with their sources and with their uncertainty stated.

This section builds on the Library's existing wax shelf rather than restarting it —
`Punic_Wax.wiki`, `Encaustic.wiki` and `Edible_Waxes_Hive_Foods_and_Aromatic_Resins.wiki`
already establish the controlling principle: '''the additive sets the melting point, and
the melting point sets the behaviour.'''

---

== 3.1 Melting points, and why temperature — not "candle" — is the only variable ==

The word "candle" tells you nothing. Two candles of the same size can differ by '''25 °C'''
in the temperature of their melt pool. The only variable that matters is '''the temperature
of the wax when it reaches skin''', and that is set by the wax's formulation.

=== The melting-point table ===

{| class="wikitable"
! Wax !! Melting point °C !! °F !! Notes
|-
| Coconut wax || ~38–43 || ~100–110 || Lowest of the common waxes; usually sold in blends
|-
| Soy container wax (e.g. GW 464) || '''45–48''' || '''113–119''' || Congealing point of generic soy container wax is quoted lower still, ~34–42 °C (ASTM D938)
|-
| Purpose-made massage-candle blends (soy/coconut + butters + oils) || ~40–50 || ~104–122 || Oils and butters are added specifically to depress the melt point
|-
| Paraffin, container grade || '''≤54''' || '''≤130''' || The industry cutoff for "low-melt / container" wax
|-
| Paraffin, votive / pillar grade || '''54–62''' || '''130–145''' || A nominal 62 °C (143 °F) grade is used where free-standing rigidity is needed
|-
| Paraffin, general range across all grades || 46–71 || 115–160 || Varies with grade and oil content
|-
| '''Beeswax''' || '''62–64''' || '''144–147''' || "Natural" does not mean cooler. Beeswax is '''near the top''' of the usable range
|-
| Carnauba || ~82–86 || ~180–187 || Hardener. Not a skin wax
|-
| Damar-hardened encaustic medium || ~80–93 || ~180–200 || 10–25% damar lifts beeswax this far. Not a skin wax
|-
| '''Punic wax (saponified beeswax)''' || '''~100''' || '''~212''' || The Library's own page documents the 60→100 °C shift. '''Never on skin.''' It is also alkaline.
|}

Sources: the soy and paraffin figures are supplier technical data and candle-industry
grade conventions (AAK GW 464 retail TDS; chemical-supply slab grades; the 54 °C
container / 54–62 °C pillar convention appears consistently across suppliers but '''is not
a formal standard''' — confirm against the data sheet for the specific wax). The beeswax,
damar and carnauba figures are the Library's own, from `Encaustic.wiki`. The Punic figure
is from `Punic_Wax.wiki` (Fritz Faiss).

'''The practical reading of that table:''' soy and coconut blends sit in a usable band.
Paraffin container wax is at the edge. Paraffin pillar wax, beeswax and everything below
it in the table are '''above the threshold at which skin blisters in under a minute'''.

=== Why those numbers matter: the thermal-injury thresholds ===

The relevant physiology is '''Henriques & Moritz 1947''' (''American Journal of Pathology''
23(4):530–549 and 23(5):695–720), still the reference work. Their findings, as reported
in the later review literature:

* '''44 °C''' held for '''5 hours''' → mild hyperaemia only. Held for '''6 hours''' → complete
  epidermal necrosis. 44 °C is the floor at which damage accumulates at all.
* '''53 °C''' for '''30 seconds''' → '''blister threshold'''.
* Between those points the relationship is '''exponential''', not linear: a small rise in
  temperature produces a large fall in the tolerable time. As a working heuristic, each
  degree above about 45 °C roughly halves the time to injury.
* '''43 °C''' is the "infinite contact" touch-temperature limit used in the standards
  (ISO 13732-1 / IEC Guide 117): below it, contact of any duration is predicted not to
  burn.

'''The conductivity caveat, which is the part usually got wrong.''' ISO 13732-1's burn
thresholds are '''material-dependent'''. Metal at 60 °C burns in a fraction of the time
that a low-conductivity material at 60 °C does, because metal delivers heat into the skin
far faster. Wax is a poor conductor, and this is the genuine physical reason wax at
temperatures that would be instantly injurious from a metal surface is survivable. That
is the real mechanism — not "wax is gentle."

'''But there is a second half to it that is usually omitted, and it cuts the other way.'''
Wax does not merely cool from its pour temperature to body temperature; it '''freezes on
the skin''', and freezing releases the '''latent heat of fusion'''. For paraffin that is
commonly quoted at '''190–210 kJ/kg''' (reported values across grades and methods range far
more widely, roughly 100–250 kJ/kg — use the grade's own data), against a specific heat
of roughly '''2–3 kJ/kg·K'''.

Work it through for 1 g of paraffin landing at 60 °C and ending at skin temperature:
* sensible heat, 60 °C → 37 °C: ≈ 2.3 kJ/kg·K × 23 K ≈ '''53 J'''
* latent heat of solidification: ≈ '''200 J'''
* total ≈ '''253 J'''

1 g of '''water''' at 60 °C cooling to 37 °C delivers 4.18 × 23 ≈ '''96 J''' and does not
freeze. So gram for gram, at the same temperature, '''wax delivers roughly two and a half
times the thermal energy of water''' — the majority of it as latent heat, released at the
moment of solidification. Low conductivity spreads that delivery out in time; it does not
reduce the total. Both facts are true and only one of them is usually stated.

'''Clinical benchmark for comparison:''' therapeutic paraffin baths used in physiotherapy
run around '''51–54 °C (125–130 °F)''' for immersion of hands and feet — thick-skinned,
well-perfused sites, under supervision, with a known wax. This is a commonly cited figure
rather than one verified here against a device standard; treat it as an order-of-magnitude
anchor and check the specific unit's specification. It is a useful upper reference point
and it is '''well above''' what is appropriate for thin skin.

=== How to actually control it ===

Height, drip rate and "about eighteen inches" are folklore controls. They are better than
nothing, and the physics behind them is real — a droplet loses heat in flight, and small
droplets lose it fast because of their surface-to-volume ratio — but the loss depends on
droplet size, ambient temperature, air movement and the wax, so the same height gives
different results on different nights.

'''The reliable control is measurement.''' A cheap infrared or probe thermometer reading
the melt pool, plus a test drop on '''your own''' inner forearm before anything else, gives
a number instead of a guess. That is the single highest-value piece of equipment in this
whole section, and it costs less than the candle.

---

== 3.2 Dyes, scents and additives: two different harms, told apart ==

The common claim is "additives make it burn hotter." That is '''half right, and the other
half is a different injury entirely'''. Both belong on the page, labelled.

'''(a) Thermal — genuinely raises the temperature'''
* '''Stearic acid''' is added to paraffin specifically to harden it and '''raise the melting
  point'''. It does exactly what it is there to do.
* '''Pillar, votive and taper formulations''' are higher-melting ''by design'', because they
  must stand up without a container. Buying "a candle" without checking the type is how
  people end up with a 60 °C pool.
* '''Hardening resins''' (damar, mastic, copal) lift beeswax from ~62 °C to 80–93 °C — the
  Library documents this on `Encaustic.wiki`. Anything containing them is a painting
  medium, not a skin material.
* '''Glass containers and large pools''' store heat and keep the pool hot near the wick. The
  wax immediately around the wick is the hottest wax in the vessel.

'''(b) Chemical — does not raise the temperature, and is the harm people actually get'''
* '''Candle dyes are not cosmetic-grade.''' They are not screened for dermal contact, several
  are known contact sensitisers, and the pigmented grades deposit particulate that
  complicates removal and can be ground into skin.
* '''Candle fragrance oils are loaded at 6–10%.''' AAK's own recommended scent load for
  GW 464 is '''7–9%'''. The maximum dermal dilution for a leave-on body product is '''1–3%'''
  (§3.5). A scented candle therefore puts fragrance on skin at '''three to nine times''' the
  dermal limit — and candle fragrance oils are formulated for ''cold and hot throw'', not
  for dermal safety, so they are not screened for sensitisers or for phototoxicity and
  routinely contain cinnamic aldehyde, eugenol, isoeugenol and oakmoss-type materials at
  levels no dermal product would carry.
* '''Wick residue.''' Carbon from the wick ends up in the pool.

'''So the honest statement is:''' a standard scented household candle is the wrong tool for
two separate reasons — it is probably the wrong ''grade'' of wax (thermal), and it is
certainly the wrong ''formulation'' (chemical). Fixing only one of those does not fix it.
A purpose-made unscented, undyed low-melt soy or coconut blend fixes both.

---

== 3.3 Distance, site and the contraindications ==

'''Skin-site sensitivity''' tracks stratum-corneum thickness, blood supply and nerve
density. Roughly, from most tolerant to least:

* '''More tolerant:''' upper back, shoulders, buttocks, outer thighs, outer arms.
* '''Less tolerant:''' chest, abdomen, flanks, inner arms, inner thighs.
* '''Thin skin — treat as a different category:''' throat and neck, inner wrist, antecubital
  fossa, breast and nipple, genitals, perineum. Thin skin reaches a given depth of injury
  at a markedly lower thermal dose.
* '''Never:''' the face and anywhere near the eyes; any mucous membrane; inside the ear; any
  cavity or depression where wax '''pools and cannot be lifted off''' — the navel is the
  classic one, and a pooled-wax burn is deeper than a drip burn because the contact time
  is far longer.

'''Hair.''' Body hair traps wax at the follicle, holds heat against the skin, and makes
removal an epilation. Shaving beforehand reduces that, but freshly shaved skin is
micro-abraded and more reactive, so it is a real trade-off rather than a free fix. Clip
rather than shave, or do it a day ahead.

'''Hard contraindications — do not, at any temperature:'''
* '''Peripheral neuropathy of any cause (diabetes above all).''' This is the most
  under-stated item on the list. The protective withdrawal reflex is the entire safety
  system, and neuropathy removes it. The injury is discovered afterwards.
* Impaired circulation, Raynaud's, lymphoedema, or any area with compromised perfusion.
* Over broken, sunburned, infected, irradiated or recently tattooed skin; over varicose
  veins; over a recent graft or scar.
* Anyone '''intoxicated''' — alcohol and most recreational drugs blunt both the withdrawal
  reflex and the ability to report. Anyone asleep or unable to communicate.
* Anyone who has taken a '''phototoxic essential oil''' topically in the last 12–18 hours
  and will be near UV (§3.5) — unrelated mechanism, same session.

'''Fire.''' Wax is a fuel and the source is an open flame. Keep alcohol, aerosols, hair
spray, solvents and loose hair away from it; keep bedding and synthetic fabrics clear; have
'''water and a damp towel within reach''' before lighting anything; never leave it burning.

'''Removal.''' Let the wax set and lift it off in sheets. Do not pull it through hair, do not
scrape, never use a blade. A plain carrier oil loosens residue — '''but read §3.4 first,
because that oil then destroys latex.'''

---

== 3.4 Aftercare for a thermal burn, and when it needs a clinician ==

Taken from NHS guidance, which is the cleanest public statement of the steps.

'''Do, immediately:'''
# '''Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.''' Start as soon as possible —
   and it is '''still worth doing up to 3 hours''' after the injury. If running water is not
   available, use cool bottled water or a wet towel.
# Remove clothing and jewellery near the area — '''but do not remove anything stuck to it.'''
# Once cooled, '''lay cling film over it. Do not wrap cling film around it''' (circumferential
   wrapping constricts as the area swells).
# Simple analgesia — paracetamol or ibuprofen.

'''Do not:'''
* '''No ice, no iced water.''' Ice causes further injury by vasoconstriction and cold damage.
* '''No creams, oils, butter, toothpaste or ointments on a fresh burn.''' This matters
  specially here, because the oil is right there on the table.
* '''Do not burst blisters.''' The blister roof is a sterile dressing.
* No plasters or sticky dressings directly on the burn.

'''Go to A&E / call emergency services if the burn:'''
* is '''very large or deep''';
* is on the '''face, genitals or bottom''';
* was caused by '''acid, another chemical, or electricity'''.

(That is the NHS list, which deliberately gives '''no numeric threshold'''.) The size and
site criteria used in burn-service referral guidance, which are a useful supplement, add:
burns larger than the patient's '''palm (~1% body surface)'''; '''full-thickness''' burns —
white, brown, charred, or leathery and '''painless''', because painlessness means the nerve
endings are gone and is a sign of a ''worse'' burn, not a better one; '''circumferential'''
burns; burns to '''hands, feet or major joints'''; any burn in a '''young child'''; and any
burn later showing '''spreading redness, increasing pain, pus or fever''' (infection).

For wax specifically: a drip burn from a correctly chosen low-melt wax is usually
superficial. A '''pooled''' wax burn, or one under a strap, cuff or waistband where the wax
was held against skin, can be partial-thickness or deeper despite a modest temperature,
because the contact time was long. Judge by the wound, not by the wax.

---

== 3.5 Massage and carrier oils ==

=== Comedogenic ratings — and the honest caveat about the scale ===

The 0–5 comedogenic scale is in universal use and is '''weak evidence'''. It derives from
the '''rabbit-ear assay''' (Kligman and colleagues; later Fulton's tables). The criticism is
not fringe:

* '''Kligman himself''', reappraising in 1996, concluded that neither the rabbit nor the
  human assay is entirely satisfactory, that petrolatum showed no comedogenic potential in
  acne patients, and that '''greasiness cannot be equated with comedogenicity'''.
* '''Frank (1982)''' found the model had many performance problems and '''lacked correlation
  with human experience'''.
* '''Mirshahpanah & Maibach (2007)''', as quoted in secondary literature, held that the model
  cannot accurately reflect acnegenic potential and is useful mainly for identifying
  '''absolute negatives'''.
* Rabbits lack human facial sebaceous-follicle biology and do not develop acne vulgaris, so
  the assay plausibly measures '''irritation''' more than comedogenesis.

So: use the chart as a '''weak prior''', and let a '''patch test''' overrule it. Published
figures also disagree between sources. With that stated:

{| class="wikitable"
! Oil / butter !! Commonly cited rating !! Oxidative stability
|-
| Argan || 0 || good (high oleic)
|-
| Hemp seed || 0 || '''poor''' — high linoleic
|-
| Safflower (high-oleic) || 0–1 || good
|-
| Grapeseed || 1 || '''poor''' — high linoleic
|-
| Castor || 1 || good, but very viscous
|-
| Sunflower || 0–2 (cultivar-dependent) || poor unless high-oleic
|-
| Shea butter || 0–2 || good
|-
| '''Jojoba''' || 2 || '''excellent — see below'''
|-
| Sweet almond || 2 || moderate
|-
| Olive || 2 || good
|-
| Apricot kernel || 2 || moderate
|-
| Avocado || 3 || good
|-
| Cocoa butter || 4 || excellent
|-
| '''Coconut (virgin)''' || '''4''' || excellent
|-
| Fractionated coconut (MCT) || low (differs from virgin) || excellent
|-
| Wheat germ || 5 || poor
|}

=== Oxidation and rancidity — the part that actually causes reactions ===

This matters more than the comedogenic number, and it is mostly ignored.

* '''Polyunsaturated (high-linoleic) oils oxidise fast''': grapeseed, sunflower, hemp,
  rosehip, wheat germ. Practical shelf life once opened is roughly '''3–6 months'''.
* '''Monounsaturated (high-oleic) oils''' — olive, sweet almond, apricot kernel, avocado,
  high-oleic sunflower — keep roughly '''a year'''.
* '''Jojoba is not a triglyceride at all.''' It is a '''liquid wax ester''', chemically much
  closer to the wax shelf than to the seed oils, and it is essentially non-rancidifying:
  '''2–5 years'''. For this application it is the obvious default. Fractionated coconut
  (MCT) is the other stable choice.
* '''Why it matters:''' rancid oil is not merely unpleasant. Lipid peroxidation produces
  '''hydroperoxides and reactive aldehydes''', and those are '''skin irritants and contact
  sensitisers'''. A great many "I reacted to that oil" reports are reactions to an oxidised
  oil, not to the oil.
* '''Controls:''' buy small, store cool, dark and airtight, decant rather than dip, add
  '''tocopherol (vitamin E) at ~0.5–1%''' as an antioxidant. '''Smell it''' — oxidised oil
  smells of crayons, putty or stale nuts.
* '''Nut allergy is real.''' Sweet almond is a tree-nut oil. Highly refined oils carry very
  little protein; '''cold-pressed oils carry more'''. Ask before using one on someone else.

=== Oils and latex — the genuine failure mode ===

This is the single most important interaction in the section, and it is well documented.

'''Voeller et al., ''Contraception'' (1989)''' — the reference study — found that '''as little
as 60 seconds' exposure of commercial latex condoms to mineral oil caused approximately a
90% decrease in condom strength''', measured as burst volume in the standard '''ISO air
burst test'''. Burst pressures also fell, less dramatically. The products tested included
ordinary consumer goods: Vaseline Intensive Care and Johnson's Baby Oil. By contrast,
'''five minutes' exposure to glycerol produced no significant effect'''.
<https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2535978/>

A later ''Southern Medical Journal'' study found baby oil cut mean burst time from near a
minute to '''about 11 seconds''' after a 5-minute exposure. (One secondary page circulates a
"70% in 60 seconds" figure; the PubMed abstract's '''90%''' is the one to use.)

'''What this means in practice:'''

{| class="wikitable"
! Material !! Oil-compatible?
|-
| '''Natural rubber latex''' (condoms, gloves, diaphragms, cervical caps, dams) || '''No''' — destroyed in ~60 s
|-
| '''Polyisoprene''' (synthetic "natural rubber" condoms) || '''No''' — same rubber chemistry, same failure
|-
| '''Polyurethane''' condoms || Yes
|-
| '''Nitrile''' condoms, gloves and dams || Yes
|-
| '''Silicone''' lubricant || Latex-safe — but degrades '''silicone toys'''
|-
| '''Water-based''' lubricant || Safe with everything
|}

The failure mode that catches people is not the obvious one. It is '''residue''': oil on
hands, on skin, on sheets, hours after the massage, then a latex condom. The sixty-second
figure means there is no safe interval and no "I wiped it off." If latex is going to be
used in a session, the oils belong '''before, elsewhere, or not at all''', and hands get
washed with soap — not wiped.

'''Related, and worth stating plainly:''' intravaginal use of oils is a different question
from topical massage. Oils are not cleared readily from the vaginal environment, and
petroleum jelly in particular has been associated with bacterial vaginosis in
observational work (Brown et al., ''Obstetrics & Gynecology'', 2013 — association, not
established causation). Cited as '''associational''', because that is what it is.

---

== 3.6 Essential oils on skin: dilution, sensitisers and phototoxicity ==

Essential oils are '''not''' carrier oils. They are concentrated volatile fractions, often
100–1000× the concentration of the same compounds in the plant, and the dermal rules are
specific.

=== Dilution ===

Drop counts assume roughly '''20 drops per mL''', which varies with viscosity and dropper
— weigh if it matters.

{| class="wikitable"
! Dilution !! Drops per 30 mL (1 fl oz) carrier !! Use
|-
| '''0.5–1%''' || 3–6 || Face, sensitive or compromised skin, elderly, children, pregnancy, and '''any first use'''
|-
| '''2%''' || 12 || Standard for general body massage and daily leave-on products
|-
| '''3%''' || 18 || Localised, short-term
|-
| '''5%''' || 30 || Spot application only, short course
|}

'''Never apply essential oils neat.''' Undiluted application is the main driver of the
sensitisation case literature, and sensitisation is '''permanent''' — once someone is
sensitised to linalool or limonene hydroperoxides, they react to that compound everywhere,
in every product, for life. The downside is not a rash; it is a lifelong allergy.

'''Never''' on mucous membranes, never intravaginally or rectally, never near the eyes. This
is not squeamishness — it is where the injuries are.

=== Phototoxicity: the furanocoumarins, and the direct line to the Library's CYP material ===

'''Maximum dermal use levels for leave-on products''' (Tisserand & Young, *Essential Oil
Safety*, 2nd ed. 2014, and the corresponding IFRA standard; figures below are from
secondary sources that cite them — '''verify against the book or the current IFRA standard
before publishing'''):

{| class="wikitable"
! Oil !! Max dermal %
|-
| Mandarin leaf || '''0.17%'''
|-
| '''Bergamot (expressed)''' || '''0.4%'''
|-
| Cumin || 0.4%
|-
| '''Lime (expressed/cold-pressed)''' || '''0.7%'''
|-
| Angelica root || 0.8%
|-
| Bitter orange (expressed) || 1.25%
|-
| '''Lemon (expressed)''' || '''2.0%'''
|-
| Grapefruit (expressed) || 4.0%
|}

Note that bergamot's limit is '''five times stricter than a routine 2% massage dilution'''.

Three facts that do the real work:

# '''Method decides it.''' '''Steam-distilled''' citrus oils are '''not''' phototoxic — the
   furanocoumarins are non-volatile and stay in the still. '''Cold-expressed''' oils carry
   them. '''Bergapten-free / FCF''' bergamot has had them stripped and is not phototoxic.
   The Library already makes this point on
   `Cold_Pressing_Expelling_and_Heat_Why_the_Same_Seed_Gives_Different_Oils.wiki`.
# '''Combinations add.''' The IFRA rule is that the sum of all furocoumarin-containing
   phototoxic ingredients, each expressed as a percentage of its own permitted level,
   '''must not exceed 100'''. Two oils each at half their limit is a full dose.
# '''Avoid UVA for 12–18 hours''' after application — sun or tanning bed. Rinse-off
   products (soap, shampoo) are not treated as a phototoxic risk.

'''The mechanism, and why this is a bridge and not a conflation.''' The Library already
documents '''bergamottin''' and '''6',7'-dihydroxybergamottin''' as the grapefruit
furanocoumarins that '''irreversibly inactivate intestinal CYP3A4''', with a 48–72 hour
recovery while the enterocytes synthesise new enzyme
(`Cytochrome_P450_System_Inhibition_and_Induction.wiki`;
`Bioavailability_Metabolic_Inhibition_and_Synergy.wiki`). '''Bergapten (5-MOP)''' is from
the same chemical family and is the principal ''dermal'' offender — but its harm runs by a
'''completely different mechanism''': it is a '''psoralen''', it intercalates DNA, and '''UVA
drives it to form interstrand crosslinks''', producing phytophotodermatitis — a genuine
chemical burn with blistering and long-lasting hyperpigmentation.

'''Same molecular family, two unrelated injuries, two different organs.''' Oral: enzyme
inactivation and drug-level multiplication. Dermal: UVA-activated DNA damage. Saying "it's
the grapefruit effect" about a bergamot burn would be wrong, and getting that distinction
right is exactly the standard the Library already holds itself to.

=== Dermal sensitisers and irritants ===

'''Strong sensitisers — keep well below standard dilution or avoid:'''
* '''Cinnamon bark and cassia''' (cinnamaldehyde) — among the strongest; Tisserand's limit is
  on the order of '''0.07%''', i.e. essentially a trace.
* '''Clove bud''' (eugenol), '''ylang-ylang''' and basil types (isoeugenol, methyl eugenol).
* '''Lemongrass and may chang''' (citral).
* '''Peru balsam''' — a classic contact allergen and a standard patch-test antigen.

'''Irritants (a different thing — dose-dependent, not immune-mediated):'''
* '''Oregano, thyme, savory''' (carvacrol, thymol) — strong mucous-membrane and skin
  irritants.
* '''Mustard, wintergreen''' — wintergreen is methyl salicylate and is systemically
  dangerous; the Library's `Scent_as_a_Drug_Route...` article notes a teaspoon is roughly
  '''7 g of aspirin'''-equivalent.

'''And the one that matters most, because it is about storage rather than identity:'''
'''oxidation'''. The autoxidation products of '''d-limonene''', '''linalool''' and
'''α-pinene''' — their '''hydroperoxides''' — are among the most frequently positive fragrance
allergens in the European baseline patch-test series. '''Tea tree''' oxidises to
'''ascaridole''', which is the sensitiser there. A fresh bottle of lavender or tea tree is
low-risk; the same bottle, opened, warm and half-empty for two years, is a different
substance. '''An old essential oil is more dangerous than a strong one.''' Buy small, keep
cold and dark, date the bottle.

=== Patch testing ===

Before a first use on anyone: mix at '''twice''' the intended use concentration, apply a
small amount to the '''inner forearm''', cover, and '''read at 48 hours'''. A reaction at 2%
means do not use at 1%. This takes two days and prevents the one outcome that cannot be
undone — permanent sensitisation.
